title: Divisibility
coreInsight: Divisibility asks whether a quantity can be partitioned into equal groups with no remainder; digit tests are consequences of place-value structure rather than magic rules.
narrativeTransition: Repeatedly sort quantities into equal groups and ask what property distinguishes the cases with no leftovers.
commonMisconceptions: Divisor, factor, and multiple are interchangeable words.
1 is prime.
A divisibility test can be applied outside the condition under which it was derived.
The remainder can be ignored when discussing divisibility.

title: Primes & Prime Factorization
coreInsight: Every positive integer greater than 1 decomposes uniquely into prime building blocks.
narrativeTransition: Keep splitting composite factors until every branch ends in an indivisible prime, then compare different-looking factor trees of the same number.
commonMisconceptions: 1 is prime.
Every odd number is prime.
Different orders of factoring produce different prime factorizations.
A composite number must have many distinct prime factors.

title: GCD & LCM
coreInsight: Prime factorization lets us compare multiplicative structure: the GCD keeps the prime powers shared by both numbers, while the LCM contains every prime power required by either.
narrativeTransition: Line up two prime-factor inventories and physically form the shared collection and the smallest collection large enough to contain both.
commonMisconceptions: GCD and LCM are easily swapped.
The LCM always equals the product of the two numbers.
Common factors and common multiples are the same kind of object.
Prime multiplicities can be ignored.

title: Factors & Divisor Counting
coreInsight: Choosing a divisor means independently choosing how many copies of each prime factor to include, so divisor counts arise from multiplying exponent-choice counts.
narrativeTransition: Move from listing factor pairs to building every factor by selecting exponents from the prime factorization.
commonMisconceptions: Only factor pairs need to be counted.
1 and the number itself can be omitted.
Exponent-choice counts should be added rather than multiplied.
Different construction orders create different divisors.

title: Remainders & Modular Arithmetic
coreInsight: When division repeats in fixed groups, only the leftover position matters; numbers with the same remainder therefore behave alike for many purposes.
narrativeTransition: Treat divisibility as the special remainder-zero case, then place all other numbers into repeating remainder classes or positions on a clock.
commonMisconceptions: A remainder may equal or exceed the divisor.
Congruence means ordinary equality.
The quotient is more important than the remainder class.
Equivalent remainder descriptions represent different modular states.

title: Units Digits & Cycles
coreInsight: The last digits of repeated powers often form periodic residue cycles, so a huge exponent can be replaced by its position in a short cycle.
narrativeTransition: Compute several successive units digits until repetition becomes visible, then use the cycle position instead of continuing the power.
commonMisconceptions: The cycle length can be assumed without checking.
Cycle positions are indexed from zero in every setup.
Every base has the same cycle length.
The exponent itself is the units digit pattern.

title: Digits, Place Value & Number Bases
coreInsight: A numeral is a weighted sum of its digits; changing the base changes the place-value weights but not the underlying positional idea.
narrativeTransition: Decompose a familiar decimal numeral into hundreds, tens, and ones, then replace 10 with a general base to reveal the structure.
commonMisconceptions: A digit and the number it appears in are the same kind of object.
A leading zero creates a genuinely new place-value length.
Digit optimization can ignore positional weights.
Base-b numerals should still be interpreted with powers of 10.
